It's September 2032. Andrei has been working at the BVG for two weeks. On Friday he has to present his first concept to the team. In the evening he rehearses in Ludwig's flat. Ludwig is the audience.
Right. “Dear colleagues, my presentation is about the question: how do passengers with disabilities find the right stop?” How does that sound?
Good. But too quiet. Right at the back there's always someone who doesn't hear well. Usually the boss.
OK, louder. “My presentation has three parts. First I'll present the results of our survey. Then I'll show the prototype. And at the end I'll talk about the next steps.”
Very orderly. Like a tram timetable. Go on.

“The chart shows how many passengers have problems getting on. What is striking is that the proportion has risen in the last ten years from twelve to eighteen per cent. This is mainly due to the fact that people are getting older.”
Eighteen per cent. That's almost one in five. Say it like that. People forget percentages, but not people.
Good idea. “That means: almost one in five passengers has difficulties. Compared with 2022, the number of wheelchair users has actually doubled.”
And then? What's your most important sentence?
I don't know. Maybe: “In future our app will show for every stop whether it's step-free.”
No. That's a technical sentence. Your most important sentence is the one people still remember on Friday evening. At dinner. Think about it.
And what was your most important sentence? In forty years?
“Bitte zurückbleiben.” (“Please stand back.”) I must have said it about a million times. And every time I waited till the last person had got on.

“von … auf …” = from… to… (values). “um …” = by… (the difference). “Von 12 auf 18 Prozent” = an increase “um 6 Prozentpunkte” (by 6 percentage points).
Fractions: die Hälfte (1/2), ein Drittel (1/3), ein Viertel (1/4), drei Viertel (3/4). “Mehr als die Hälfte der Befragten…” = more than half of those asked…

On Friday morning, eighteen people were sitting in the big meeting room on the sixth floor of the BVG headquarters: programmers, designers, two people from management, a representative of the passengers' association, Kurt Wolff from the museum. And in the front row, with his stick between his knees and a visitor's badge on his jacket, sat Ludwig. Mrs Demir had invited him personally. “As an expert,” she had said on the phone. “For what no software knows.” For the first time since Ingrid's funeral, Ludwig had put on a tie. By himself. It had taken twenty minutes.

Andrei had spent his first two weeks at the BVG in a kind of fog. New colleagues, new programs, an office with a view of the Spree, a coffee machine that only spat out water, and meetings with so many abbreviations that he sometimes felt as if he were in his first month in Berlin. Timo, the programmer with the beard, had written him a list on his second day: “The hundred most important BVG abbreviations.” Andrei had learned them by heart in bed in the evenings, like irregular verbs in the old days. Lena had tested him and nearly died laughing.

Andrei stood at the front, next to a big screen, and hadn't said a word since six in the morning. The evening before he had rehearsed the presentation three more times in front of Ludwig, then twice in front of Lena, who had fallen asleep at some point, and once alone, in front of the bathroom mirror, at two in the morning. Now, in front of eighteen faces, he felt as if he had forgotten everything. He looked at Ludwig. Ludwig raised his stick a centimetre, like a conductor giving the cue. And Andrei began.

The first part went well. He presented the survey, twelve thousand passengers, asked in the spring. He showed the chart with the red line rising from the bottom left to the top right, from twelve to eighteen per cent. “That means,” he said, and now he was speaking loudly enough for the boss in the back row, “that almost one in five people standing at one of our stops doesn't know whether they can get on.” He saw two programmers writing something down. He saw Kurt Wolff nodding.

Then he showed the second chart, a pie chart in four colours: what do passengers with disabilities want most? More than half had answered: real-time information. A quarter: more lifts. The rest: friendlier staff and more seats at the stops. “What is striking,” said Andrei, “is that only five per cent want a new app. People don't want a new app. They want the old one to finally tell them what they need to know.” A few people laughed. Mrs Demir smiled and wrote something down.

The second part, the prototype, went less well. The demo on the laptop crashed, exactly at the moment when he wanted to show how the app displays the height of the step for each stop. A black screen, eighteen people, total silence. Andrei felt the blood rush to his head. One of the programmers, a young man with a beard called Timo, whispered: “It happens to everyone. Twice to me last week.” Andrei restarted the laptop. It took two minutes. They were the longest two minutes of his life.

And in those two minutes something happened that wasn't in the plan. Ludwig stood up, slowly, leaning on his stick, turned to the eighteen people and said: “May I use the time? I'm the passenger in the chart. One of the eighteen per cent.” Mrs Demir nodded. And Ludwig spoke, without slides, without notes, in his deep, calm voice that had announced the stops for forty years.

I drove trams for forty-one years. I know every stop in this city. And for a year I haven't ridden them. Not because I don't want to. But because I stand at the stop and don't know whether the tram that's coming is an old one with three steps or a new one with no steps. If it's the old one, I can't manage it. And then I stand there, in front of the open door, and behind me people are waiting, and the driver is waiting, and I have to say: go on, don't worry. I'll take the next one. Do you know what that's like? For a man who has said a million times: please stand back?

He sat down again. Nobody said anything. Kurt Wolff was looking at the table. Then the man in the wheelchair said quietly, but so that everyone could hear: “That's exactly how it is. Only I can't take the next tram either. Or the one after that. Sometimes I sit there for half an hour waiting for a new one to come.” Andrei saw one of the gentlemen from management, who until then had been looking at his phone, put his phone away.

The room was quiet. Nobody was typing any more. The representative of the passengers' association, a man in a wheelchair, had stopped taking notes. Then the screen came on again, and Andrei showed the demo, and this time it worked: a map of Prenzlauer Berg, every stop with a little symbol, green for step-free, yellow for partly, red for steps. And underneath, for every tram arriving, a little sign: old or new tram, with or without steps, in three minutes, in seven minutes.

At the end I'd like to leave you with a single sentence. Not mine. Mr Brandt's. A tram doesn't run for the driver, but for the passenger who gets on most slowly. Our app should do the same. Thank you for your attention.

The applause didn't come straight away. Kurt Wolff was the first to clap, slowly, loudly. Then the man in the wheelchair. Then everyone. Mrs Demir stood up, went over to Andrei, shook his hand and said, so that everyone could hear: “Mr Ionescu, I've seen a lot of presentations in fifteen years. Yours wasn't the most perfect. The laptop crashed and once you said the number had ‘risen to twelve per cent’ instead of ‘from twelve’. But it was the first one I'll still remember at dinner tonight.”

After the presentation the gentleman from management who had put his phone away came over to them. He introduced himself as Dr Hartmann, head of the passenger information department. He shook Ludwig's hand first, then Andrei's. “I've learned something today,” he said. “For three years we've talked about accessibility, in meetings, with slides and tables. But nobody has ever explained to us what it's like to stand in front of an open door and not be able to get on.” He looked at Andrei. “You'll get the budget. And two more programmers. I want to see the app in the test phase by Christmas.”

Timo came over last and patted Andrei on the shoulder. “The crash was the best thing that could have happened to you,” he said. “Without it, Mr Brandt would never have spoken. Maybe you should include it in every presentation.” Andrei laughed, for the first time that day. And Ludwig, who was just handing in his visitor's badge, said to Timo: “Young man, in forty years I've learned this: the best runs are never the ones that go according to the timetable. They're the ones where something goes wrong and everyone finds a solution together.” Timo wrote the sentence on a note and stuck it on his monitor. As far as anyone knows, it's still hanging there today.

In the afternoon they went home together, Andrei and Ludwig. By tram. Andrei had the new test version of the app on his phone, and they stood at the stop at Alexanderplatz looking at the little screen: M2, new tram, no steps, in four minutes. Ludwig waited. The tram came, long, white and yellow, and stopped, and the floor of the tram was exactly level with the pavement. Ludwig got on, without help, without hesitating. He sat down by the window. And when the doors closed and the driver, a young man with headphones round his neck, said over the loudspeaker: “Bitte zurückbleiben”, Ludwig put his hand on his chest and closed his eyes, and Andrei saw that he was smiling.

At Alexanderplatz, under the TV Tower, Ludwig stopped for a moment and looked around. “This used to be my terminus,” he said. “In 1974, on the number 46. Ingrid often waited for me here after school, with a book, on the bench over there. The bench isn't there any more. But the place is still the same.”
